title: The Tent at Ji‘ranah • The Weeping of the Ansar • The Delegates of Hawazin • A Complaint in the Name of Justice

blocks.1: Returning from Ta’if, the Prophet {{1}} halted at Ji‘ranah, where the spoils of Hunayn had been kept. Six thousand prisoners, twenty-four thousand camels, more than forty thousand goats, four thousand uqiyyah of silver. He did not distribute them. He waited more than ten nights. The thought was, if anyone of Hawazin came repenting, he would return their wealth. No one came. Then the distribution began.{{2}}
blocks.2: The first to be called were the chiefs of Makkah, who had only just come into Islam. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb (RA), Safwan ibn Umayyah, ‘Uyaynah ibn Hisn and Aqra‘ ibn Habis, each received a hundred camels. ‘Abbas ibn Mirdas received less than that. He said in verse,
blocks.4: Will you divide the plunder of me and of my companions between ‘Uyaynah and al-Aqra‘?{{1}}
blocks.5: The Prophet {{1}} completed his hundred too. Now about Safwan. To Safwan the Prophet {{2}} gave a hundred, again a hundred, again a hundred, three hundred camels in all. Later Safwan (RA) used to say,
blocks.7: By Allah, what the Prophet {{1}} gave me, he gave at a time when he was the most disliked of people to me. He kept giving until he became the dearest of people to me.{{2}}
blocks.8: The one who is not gathering this wealth but giving it away, the reason for his giving he himself has stated,
blocks.10: I give to Quraysh to win their hearts, because they have only just come up out of Jahiliyyah.{{1}}
blocks.11: For one who has only just come up from shirk, the smallest way to pull him up by the hand is perhaps a gift. For a man whose house and honour have been broken, before the question, honour comes first. The man Safwan disliked most, by giving and giving, that very man became dearest to him. The bedouins, hoping for goods, crowded around the Prophet {{1}}. Pushing and pushing they took him to a thorn tree. His cloak caught in the tree’s thorns. He stood and said,
blocks.13: Give me my cloak. By Allah, if I had camels equal in number to these thorn trees, I would distribute all of them among you. Then you would find me neither stingy, nor a liar, nor a coward.{{1}}
blocks.14: Then he plucked a tuft of wool from his camel’s hump, held it in his hand and said, people, not even this bit of wool is mine. Then he said,
blocks.16: Of the fay’ that Allah has given you, my share is only the fifth; and that fifth too is returned among you.{{1}}
blocks.17: One who pays such a price when giving is this detached about his own share. The cloak caught in the thorn tree too he gives, but not even his bit of wool. For the one into whose hand wealth comes, the test is exactly here. For one to whom rank and wealth are places of service, he settles others’ shares before taking his own. The foot soldiers got four camels or forty goats; the horsemen got three times that. Zayd ibn Thabit (RA) gathered everyone and explained the accounts.
blocks.19: There was a gap in that distribution at Ji‘ranah. The chiefs of Makkah got a hundred camels each. The Ansar got nothing at all. The Ansar who had sheltered the Prophet {{1}} in the face of the swords of Makkah’s enemies, whose swords had flashed at Hunayn too. Some young men of the Ansar whispered among themselves, may Allah forgive the Prophet {{2}}, he is giving to the Quraysh, leaving us out, though their blood still drips from our swords. The word reached the ears of Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubadah (RA). He came and told the Prophet {{3}}. The Prophet {{4}} asked, what is your own view about this? Sa‘d said, I am only one of my people. The Prophet {{5}} said, gather your people in this place. In a leather tent only the Ansar were gathered. A few Muhajirun came, they were not allowed to enter. When all had gathered the Prophet {{6}} came and asked, what word has come to me from you? The elder jurists of the Ansar said, O Messenger of Allah, our leaders said nothing. But a few young ones have said such a thing. The Prophet {{7}}, praising Allah, said,
blocks.21: O people of the Ansar! What is this word of yours that has reached me? Did I not find you astray, and Allah guided you through me? You were divided, and Allah united you through me? You were needy, and Allah enriched you through me?{{1}}
blocks.22: Each time he asked a question, the Ansar said in reply, Allah and His Messenger are more gracious. Then he said, if you wish you can say this too: you came to us in a state when you were being called a liar, we affirmed you as truthful; you came helpless, we helped you; you had been driven out, we sheltered you; you were in need, we comforted you. By Allah, if you say this you will be telling the truth, and your word will be accepted as true.{{1}}
blocks.23: Then he explained the reason for his decision. Quraysh had only just come from Jahiliyyah and calamity. He had wanted to make up their loss, to win their hearts. Then he said,
blocks.25: Are you not satisfied that people go back with goats and camels, and you go back to your homes with the Prophet {{1}}? By Allah, what you are returning with is better than what they are returning with.{{2}}
blocks.28: If all the people go into one valley and the Ansar into another mountain pass, I would choose the pass of the Ansar.{{1}}
blocks.29: The Ansar began to weep. Weeping, their beards were soaked. They said, we are satisfied with the Messenger of Allah {{1}}. The Prophet {{2}} then said, O Allah, have mercy on the Ansar, on the children of the Ansar, and on the children of their children. The Prophet {{3}} left the gathering. The people went back, each to his own. This incident is arranged in five steps. First, hearts were broken, this news reached him; Sa‘d did not suppress the word. Second, he did not wait, thinking it would be fine as time passed; that very day he called them and gathered everyone. Third, only the Ansar, no outsider. In a private meeting the complainers do not have to be ashamed. The fourth step is harder still. He himself composed, on the Ansar’s behalf, the very language of the complaint, and said, if you say this you will be telling the truth. The one against whom the complaint is, he himself said the strongest word of the complainers. Where is this courtesy today? The fifth step, not wealth, he gave himself. I am yours, my life is your life. He explained why that day he had given wealth to the new people of Makkah, and put into the Ansar’s hands what cannot be bought with wealth: himself. We often think, someone’s heart has been broken, it will be fine as time passes. What time can do is make the broken place set hard, joined wrongly. The decision is mine, taken with good intention. But how it felt to the one on whom the shadow of that decision has fallen, I will not know unless I ask.
blocks.31: In the meantime a delegation of fourteen from Hawazin arrived as Muslims. Their leader was Zuhayr ibn Surad. Among them was a milk-uncle of the Prophet {{1}}, Abu Burqan. They took the pledge and said, O Messenger of Allah, among those you have taken captive are our mothers, sisters, paternal aunts and maternal aunts. This is a great humiliation for us. They said in verse, be gracious to us, you are a man from whom hope can be held; have mercy on the women whose milk you once drank. Among these captives was the Prophet’s {{2}} milk-sister Shayma’ bint al-Harith (RA). She came to the Prophet {{3}} and gave her identity, the Prophet {{4}} spread out his cloak and seated her with honour, then graciously sent her back. That story will come in full in Dars 27.{{5}}
blocks.32: The Prophet {{1}} said to the delegation, the people you see with me, the dearest word to me is the true word. So say, which is dearer to you, children and women, or wealth?
blocks.34: The dearest word to me is the true word.{{1}}
blocks.35: They said, nothing is dearer to us than lineage and honour. The Prophet {{1}} said, after the Zuhr prayer you stand and say, we make the Messenger of Allah an intercessor with the believers, and the believers with the Messenger of Allah. They did so. The Prophet {{2}} said, what has fallen to my share and that of Banu ‘Abd al-Muttalib is given to you; from the others too I will ask for you. The Muhajirun and the Ansar at once stood up and said, everything of our share is for the Messenger of Allah. But Aqra‘ ibn Habis and ‘Uyaynah ibn Hisn, the two chiefs, said, we will not give our share. Nor ‘Abbas ibn Mirdas. Banu Sulaym said, everything of ours is for the Messenger of Allah. Then ‘Abbas ibn Mirdas said, you have struck my honour dead! The Prophet {{3}} said, they have come as Muslims. It was for them that I delayed the distribution. If any of you has a captive, if he gives gladly, good. And whoever wants to keep his share must return that too. In exchange, in the first victory that comes ahead, I will give six in place of one. All together the announcement was made. Everyone agreed to return the captives. In the end ‘Uyaynah too agreed.{{4}}
blocks.36: Where not everyone agreed, the Prophet {{1}} did not force. He said, I do not know which of you gives gladly and which does not. So go back. Your representatives will come and tell me.
blocks.38: We do not know who among you has consented and who has not. So go back, let your representatives convey your opinion to us.{{1}}
blocks.39: When wealth that people had won by fighting had to be returned, the Prophet {{1}} gave as much as he could from his own and asked the rest; but he did not put his hand over anyone’s mouth. Not silent consent, but confirmation through a representative. Where someone has a right, no decision without hearing everyone’s voice. The commander of Hawazin, Malik ibn ‘Awf, was hiding in the fortress of Ta’if. The Prophet {{2}} sent word, if he comes as a Muslim, he will get back his family and wealth, and a hundred camels besides. Malik came out secretly and accepted Islam. The very man who at Hunayn had raised the sword in front of the Muslims later wrote his name in history as a heroic commander of Islam.{{3}}
blocks.40: The Qur’an had told of that moment beforehand. Right after speaking of the punishment at Hunayn,
blocks.42: Then after that Allah grants repentance to whom He wills. Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.{{1}}
blocks.43: The one from whom we are being hurt today may tomorrow be our most trusted companion. For whom Allah will open the door of repentance, I do not know. My task is to keep my own door open.
blocks.44: A Complaint in the Name of Justice
blocks.45: At Ji‘ranah the silver was then being distributed. Silver in Bilal’s (RA) cloth; the Prophet {{1}} was taking handfuls from it and giving to people. From the crowd a man came and stood. He said, Muhammad, be just. The Prophet {{2}} said,
blocks.47: Woe to you! If I do not do justice, then who will do justice? If I do not do justice, then you have failed and lost.{{1}}
blocks.48: Hearing the word ‘Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA) said, O Messenger of Allah, let me go, I will strike off this hypocrite’s neck. The Prophet {{1}} said,
blocks.50: Allah forbid! Let people not say that I kill my companions. This man and his companions will recite the Qur’an, it will not go below their throats. They will leave the religion as an arrow passes through the game.{{1}}
blocks.51: The man’s name was Dhu al-Khuwaysirah, of Banu Tamim. He had not come as an enemy of the Muslims. He had come thinking himself a man on the side of justice. But the Prophet’s {{1}} reckoning of justice did not seem right in his eyes. When saying it, on his lips was the appeal to justice, and inside, the audacity to put the Prophet {{2}} on trial. The Prophet {{3}} warned at once, next to the prayer of his companions you will think your own prayer small. But it will not cross their throats. Many years later a man with that mark was found in the battle of Nahrawan with ‘Ali (RA), and Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (RA) was a witness.{{4}}
blocks.52: Why did he not let Dhu al-Khuwaysirah be killed? ‘People will say, Muhammad kills his companions.’ Even when harsh words were spoken directly against himself, his concern was not about his own dignity; it was about people’s trust in Islam. And at the same time he also told the sign of a future fitnah: those whose prayer and fasting will shame you, they will recite the Qur’an, yet leave the religion. From seeing prayer and Qur’an, someone’s being on the truth is not proved. And again, seeing sarcasm in the name of justice, someone’s intention cannot be caught either. The measure is only one: how he stands before the Messenger. A complaint in which there is no humility has little justice, much arrogance.

footnotes.0: Sahih al-Bukhari 4318 (from Marwan ibn al-Hakam and Miswar ibn Makhramah (RA); ‘on returning from Ta’if the Prophet {{1}} kept them waiting more than ten nights’: ‘wa kana anzarahum bid‘a ‘ashrata laylah’); al-Rahiq al-Makhtum, pp. 687–688 (Sirah-based: the spoils: six thousand prisoners, twenty-four thousand camels, more than forty thousand goats, four thousand uqiyyah of silver; kept at Ji‘ranah under the supervision of Mas‘ud ibn ‘Amr al-Ghifari; distribution through Zayd ibn Thabit: foot soldier four camels or forty goats, horseman twelve camels or a hundred and twenty goats). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.1: Sahih Muslim 1060 (from Rafi‘ ibn Khadij (RA); sahih): ‘The Prophet {{1}} gave Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Safwan ibn Umayyah, ‘Uyaynah ibn Hisn and Aqra‘ ibn Habis a hundred camels each, to ‘Abbas ibn Mirdas less than this. ‘Abbas ibn Mirdas said, ... so the Prophet {{2}} completed his hundred too.’ The last line of the poem: ‘wa man takhfidi al-yawma la yurfa‘’ (the one who is lowered today does not rise again).
footnotes.2: Sahih Muslim 2313 (Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri ← Sa‘id ibn al-Musayyab ← Safwan ibn Umayyah; sahih). Safwan was given that day in three rounds, a hundred-a-hundred-a-hundred camels. In Ahmad (Arna’ut: sahih) and Jami‘ al-Tirmidhi 666 (al-Albani: sahih) too there is a narration of the same sense.
footnotes.3: Sahih al-Bukhari 3146 (from Anas (RA); sahih); in Sahih al-Bukhari 4334, Anas (RA): ‘Quraysh have only just come from Jahiliyyah and calamity; I wanted to make up their loss and win their hearts.’ This is called ‘i‘anat al-mu’allafati qulubuhum’ (Surah al-Tawbah 9:60).
footnotes.4: Sahih al-Bukhari 3148 (from Jubayr ibn Mut‘im (RA); sahih): ‘On returning from Hunayn the bedouins crowded around the Prophet {{1}}, asking and asking, pushed him toward an acacia tree; his cloak caught on the tree.’ ‘Al-‘idah’: thorny trees.
footnotes.5: Sahih al-Jami‘ 7872 (al-Albani: sahih); Irwa’ al-Ghalil 1240 (al-Albani: sahih). The same statement is in al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (p. 688), taking a tuft of wool from the camel’s hump and saying: ‘not even this bit of wool is mine, only the fifth; that too is yours.’ (Sirah-based part).
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari 4330 (from ‘Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn ‘Asim (RA); sahih); Sahih Muslim 1061 (the same narration). Each time the Prophet {{1}} asked a question, the Ansar would say, ‘Allah and His Messenger are more gracious.’ ‘Dallal’: astray, ‘‘alah’: poor.
footnotes.7: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 688–690 (Ibn Ishaq via Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (RA): Sa‘d ibn ‘Ubadah (RA) informed the Prophet {{1}} and said, ‘I am one of my people’; the Prophet {{2}} said, ‘call your people’; when some Muhajirun came, he did not let them in; the speech about the Ansar: ‘you came to us in a state when you were being called a liar…’, ‘may Allah have mercy on the Ansar, on the children of the Ansar…’; their beards becoming wet with tears). A combined account of a sahih chain and the Sirah. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.8: Sahih al-Bukhari 4331, 4334 (from Anas (RA); sahih); Sahih Muslim 1059 (the same incident). The Prophet {{1}} ordered patience for the Ansar, saying that in later life there would come ‘athara’ (others being preferred over them); Anas (RA) says, ‘but they could not be patient’ (Bukhari 4331).
footnotes.9: Sahih al-Bukhari 4333 (from Anas (RA)); 4330; Sahih Muslim 1061 (also: ‘had it not been for hijrah I would have been one of the Ansar’; ‘the Ansar are the shi‘ar (the garment next to the body), others the dithar (the outer garment)’).
footnotes.10: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), p. 684 (the milk-sister Shayma’ bint al-Harith al-Sa‘diyyah among the captives; she gives her identity, the Prophet {{1}} recognises her on being shown a certain mark; spreads a cloak and seats her; graciously sends her back to her people). This incident is in Dars 27 (‘Uncle, Aunt and Milk-Mother’); here only a one-line bridge. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.12: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 690–692 (the delegation of fourteen, leader Zuhayr ibn Surad, among them the Prophet’s {{1}} milk-uncle Abu Burqan; the poem ‘umnun ‘alayna Rasul Allah fi karam’; the Prophet’s {{2}} reply ‘what has fallen to my share and that of Banu ‘Abd al-Muttalib is yours’; the objection and consent of Aqra‘ ibn Habis, ‘Uyaynah ibn Hisn and ‘Abbas ibn Mirdas; the promise of six camels for each prisoner in the first victory; returning all the prisoners each with a Coptic cloth; Bukhari 2/620–621, 5/201). In Bukhari 4318 the basic announcement of returning the prisoners is sahih; the number six camels and the poem are Sirah-based. Whether the delegation came before or after the distribution of the spoils, the sources differ: in Bukhari 4318 the Prophet {{3}} gave the announcement of returning the prisoners when they came after he had waited more than ten nights for them, in al-Rahiq (p. 690) at the end of the distribution of the spoils. Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.13: Sahih al-Bukhari 4318 (final part): ‘farji‘u hatta yarfa‘a ilayna ‘urafa’ukum amrakum’; then the representatives spoke with everyone and reported, everyone had agreed gladly.
footnotes.14: Sirah-based: Ibn Ishaq ← Ibn Hisham, Ghazwat Hunayn (Malik ibn ‘Awf al-Nasri came secretly from Ta’if and accepted Islam; the Prophet {{1}} returned his family and wealth and gave him a gift of a hundred camels; made him the amir of the Muslims of his tribe). Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, note 21 on 9:27 (p. 531, reading the printed page): ‘Their leader Malik ibn ‘Awf himself too believed and he gained fame as a heroic commander of Islam.’ Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.15: Tawdih al-Qur’an, vol. 1, Surah al-Tawbah 9:27, p. 531 (matched word for word by reading the printed page); note 21: ‘This verse hints that many of those of Hawazin who had come to fight with immense valour would get the grace of repenting and believing. So it happened; a vast number of Banu Hawazin and Banu Thaqif accepted Islam later.’
footnotes.16: Sahih Muslim 1063 (from Jabir ibn ‘Abdillah (RA); sahih): ‘After returning from Hunayn at Ji‘ranah a man came to the Prophet {{1}}; Bilal’s cloth then held silver, the Prophet {{2}} was taking handfuls from it and giving to people; he said, Muhammad, be just…’. In Sahih al-Bukhari 3610 (from Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (RA)) the man’s name is ‘Dhu al-Khuwaysirah, of Banu Tamim’. ‘Khibta wa khasirta’: each of the two verbs means ‘failed’ and ‘lost’.
footnotes.17: Sahih Muslim 1063; Sahih al-Bukhari 3610 (Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (RA): ‘one of you will think his own prayer small compared with theirs, his fasting compared with theirs; they will recite the Qur’an, it will not pass their throats; they will leave the religion as an arrow passes through the game; their sign is a black man, one of whose arms is like a woman’s breast…’). Abu Sa‘id (RA) testifies that ‘Ali (RA) fought them (at Nahrawan), he was with him; the man was sought out and brought, he matched the sign described by the Prophet {{1}}.
footnotes.18: Sahih Muslim 1063; Sahih al-Bukhari 3610 (Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (RA)). The incident began at Ji‘ranah; the fitnah of the Khawarij was in the caliphate of ‘Ali (RA) (Nahrawan, 38 AH). In the dars, for the sake of the narration, the incidents are told together.

quiz.q: How many nights did the Prophet ﷺ wait before the distribution of the spoils at Ji‘ranah?
How many camels in all did the Prophet ﷺ give Safwan ibn Umayyah?
quiz.e: In three rounds, a hundred-a-hundred-a-hundred; Muslim 2313.

quiz.q: In the bedouins’ crowd at Ji‘ranah, which item of the Prophet’s ﷺ got caught in the tree’s thorns?
‘I give to Quraysh to win their hearts’; what is the purpose of this gift?
o: To buy off the leaders of Quraysh
An effort to pull them up

quiz.q: What does the incident of the Prophet ﷺ taking a tuft of wool in his hand when wealth came into hand teach?
quiz.e: Even the fifth is returned to you.

quiz.q: Winning over, with a gift, the man who dislikes you most; which incident matches this?
o: Abu Bakrah’s coming down by pulley
The death of Duraid at Awtas

quiz.q: Restraint about one’s own share when power or funds come into hand; which picture matches this?
o: Setting up a catapult at Ta’if
Taking the tuft of wool in hand

quiz.q: Who came and told the Prophet ﷺ the Ansar’s word?

o: On the roof of the Ka‘bah

quiz.q: In the incident of the Ansar’s hurt hearts, what did the Prophet ﷺ do first?
o: Gathered them privately that very day
Arranged a separate punishment for the young men

quiz.q: Learning that your decision has hurt someone’s heart, what should you do?
o: Call them aside, explain and listen to them
Leave it, thinking it will be fine as time passes

quiz.q: How many were in the delegation of Hawazin?
Who was the Prophet’s ﷺ milk-sister among the captives of Hawazin?
‘I do not know which of you gives gladly’; what does taking consent through a representative teach?
o: Making sure of the rightful ones’ consent
One can take by force even without right

quiz.q: Malik ibn ‘Awf’s accepting Islam fulfils the hint of which verse?
When a decision is bound up with the rights of many, which incident gives guidance?
o: The new Muslims’ request at Dhat Anwat
Looking for a witness to the salab

quiz.q: Dhu al-Khuwaysirah belonged to which tribe?
Why did the Prophet ﷺ not let Dhu al-Khuwaysirah be killed?
o: People would say he kills his own companions

quiz.q: Someone, saying ‘be just’ without humility, raises an objection to your decision; which incident is a warning for this?
